en: Prosperity!
Salutations to the illustrious Śrīnivāsa, the Supreme Brahman.
The Fourth Chapter of the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*:
Now, it may be argued that even though God’s knowledge exists, it is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because it lacks the defining characteristics thereof.
Because it is of such a nature as to reach an object not previously apprehended;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even memory would possess the status of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*). Furthermore, for that which is eternal and has all things as its object, there can be no such thing as an "unapprehended object."

Because of contradiction—here it is said: "The definition [of perception] is not [valid], as it is either under-extensive, over-extensive, or does not include the first instance of seeing; valid cognition is held to be a cognition of an object as it is, by virtue of its independence. (1)
For it is not the case that, when an object has been apprehended, the very act of apprehension does not arise,
since there is no obstruction to its causes;
nor is it the case that, even though it arises, it is not a valid cognition (*pramā*) because it is not required by the cognizer.
Because validity does not depend upon that [subsequent cognition];

nor does invalidity follow merely from being indistinguishable from what preceded it, for that would entail the consequence that the preceding cognition is also invalid simply because it is indistinguishable from what follows.

If, however, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇya*) were independent of that [subsequent cognition], then the same would apply to what follows it as well, since there is no distinction. Furthermore,

it is not the case that once [an object] has been determined, the eyes and other [senses] lack the status of being the most effective instruments (*sādhakatamatva*), just as axes and other tools do once the wood has been cut.
[This is] because there is a distinction based on the production or non-production of a result.

If it is argued that "that result is not indeed valid cognition (*pramā*), because its object is merely what has been previously apprehended, like memory," we say no—because if the probandum is the negation of being a "correct experience of an object" (*yathārthānubhava*), the argument is contradicted (*bādhita*);
and if the negation is of something else, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
And because it is equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*);
for, in the negation of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is conditioned by the absence of its cause, and because it is sublated (*bādhita*).
Nor is the mere fact of apprehending an unapprehended object the cause [of its being valid],
for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of treating even error as valid cognition;
nor is it this very factor qualified by the condition of being "in accordance with reality" (yathārthatva).
Because there is no pervasion by a cognition that carries on in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhana-buddhi*).

Nor can it be maintained that even in such cases, the cognition possesses the quality of apprehending an object not previously known (*anadhigatārtha-gantṛtva*), by virtue of being qualified by each respective moment of time.
This is because the limiting adjuncts of the moments cannot be apprehended.
Nor should it be imagined that a qualified state produced by those [adjuncts] manifests even when the qualifiers themselves are unknown;
for if that were produced by its own nature, it would contradict the experience of being qualified by the future and so forth.
However, if that [cognition] were produced by the cognition of that [qualifier], then in the absence of knowledge of the sun’s motion and so forth, the state of being qualified by it would not arise;
yet there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this.

Now, if the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) were to exist between two things that neither benefit nor are benefited by one another, how could the resulting over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) be avoided?
By means of making known the exclusion;
[this occurs] through its own nature in the case of exclusion;
otherwise, in that [case], it would not [be so].
"Because of the lack of a fixed rule" (vyanavasthānāt).
If it is argued that "the state of being known" (jñātatā) itself is the limiting condition (upādhi), we say no; for that will be refuted later.
Or, even if that were to exist, it would follow that memory (smṛti) would likewise possess validity (prāmāṇya).
Even though [the object] is not within the range of the sense organs, it appears as "cognized" (*jñātatā*) produced by each preceding recollection within each subsequent recollection.
Or, let it be as it may regarding perception;
what is the situation regarding the hearing of an object that was previously grasped but now forgotten?
If it is argued that this [Veda] is simply invalid, then all hope for the authority of the Veda is now lost;
for in this beginningless saṃsāra, the meaning of the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" has not been understood by anyone [prior to the Veda itself].
Even in the case of doubt, there is doubt regarding its validity;
furthermore, even in that case, specific temporal moments do not manifest clearly. Nor is this definition intended to be restricted by the convention of being delimited to a single lifetime.
For even in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of invalidity with respect to one who has experienced but forgotten the meaning of the Veda.
How, then, is memory excluded?
Simply by its being non-experience (*ananubhava*).
For the authorities on epistemology observe that valid cognition (*pramā*) is indeed an experience that accords with reality, as indicated by the aphorism: "From the knowledge of truth... (NS 1.1.1).
And [it is defined as] "non-erroneous knowledge.

Now, one might object: why should memory not be considered valid cognition (*pramā*) itself, since it is a cognition that accords with reality (*yathārthajñāna*), just like perception and other forms of direct experience?
This is not so, because once linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is established, one subsequently seeks its etymological basis.
Nor can worldly convention be regulated by a cause arbitrarily imagined by oneself,
for that would lead to the collapse of worldly conventions due to a lack of fixed standards.
Furthermore, this is not the case for those engaged in the practice of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the causes of memory.
The great sages do employ the convention of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
for they have not taught them separately.

If it is argued that they were not taught because they are not included among those already mentioned, we say no; for it is impossible for perception (*pratyakṣa*) to have a result that is not direct apprehension (*asākṣātkāra*).
And because words such as "linga" (inferential mark) do not establish cognition by their mere existence;

this being the case, it is further considered: since this [inference], having experience alone as its object, conforms to the validity or invalidity of that [experience] by looking toward its face, it is impossible to function as being valid without first establishing the validity of that [experience]. (215)
Thus, even in the case of empirical usage, it is only the prior experience that constitutes valid cognition (pramiti),
because it is independent;
it is not, however, memory (smṛti).
Because it always depends upon that [perception].
For when the experience is incorrect, the memory is likewise so.
But if this were the case, would not inference also result in being invalid?
Because it conforms to fundamental perception;
it is not [unreliable] due to a difference in object.
In that case, scripture would not be a means of valid cognition.
Because it conforms to another means of knowledge regarding that same object;
no, because the cognizers are different.
In that case, successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-buddhi*) are not valid knowledge, because they conform to the initial valid knowledge.
No, because even for the subsequent ones, as in the case of the first, there is no looking toward the preceding one merely by virtue of the purity of the cause;
rather, the sequence is a matter of coincidence (*kākatālīya*) resulting from the power of the causes.
For if—[if that were so]—then...
Memory is not a valid cognition (*pramiti*);
for what is the proof regarding the prior experience?
If it is argued that it is the "otherwise-unaccountability of memory" (*smṛty-anyathānupapatti*), we say no—because by that [argument] only a cause in general is established.
However, there is no restrictive rule that it must necessarily be produced by that very experience.
If it is argued, "In that case, memory would occur even for what has not been experienced," why should it not?
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this [position].
If it is argued that the recollection of memory is seen to have the form of a prior experience,
and that this would not be possible otherwise— then do you also, like the Buddhists, accept the establishment of an object based on the impossibility of the object's form being otherwise?
Or is that accomplishment [of the object] simply knowledge of such a nature?
In the first case, there is the same inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) as before;
for knowledge does not possess the very form of the object.
The rule that "it (perception) is preceded by that (sensation)" is not tenable, because it is subject to deviation in the case of knowledge of the future and in the case of error.
And in the second [case]...
The validity of memory is unavoidable. If it is argued, "Let there be no establishment of a prior experience;
what is lost to us?"—then the causal relationship between memory and experience would not be established.
No; for even if that [memory] were invalid, its occurrence is established precisely by the validity of the self-recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the self across prior and subsequent states.
There exists a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) in the form: "I who experienced this object am the same I who now remembers it."

Nor does the knowledge of the Lord possess the character of apprehending what has already been apprehended, because the entire universe is not within the range of any other cognition belonging to Him.
Furthermore, that very same cognition does not become invalid due to a difference in time.
Because independence does not cease;
or else, if there were invalidity in that way, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This might be argued: [it is] non-beneficial (216).

The object cannot belong to that [subject] or to this [subject], because there is no distinction [between them]. Nor can "belonging to that" be an indeterminate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding it,
because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, the production of that benefit does not occur without the cognition of it,
because such a thing is not admitted.
Or, even if [the causal relationship] were accepted, the reason "being an effect" (kāryatva) would be inconclusive.
To this it is replied: [Kārikā 4.512] "Because there is no restriction on intrinsic nature (svabhāva), even assistance (upakāra) is difficult to establish."
Even if [the cognition] were easily produced when the object exists, what would be the case otherwise? //2//

Because there is no distinction [between them], it would be untenable to maintain the restriction that the result occurs only there and not elsewhere; and if such a restriction is established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the determination of the object (*viṣaya*) is likewise established in that very same manner. Furthermore, this must necessarily be accepted...
It must be understood [in this way], in accordance with the fact that [cognition] has the past and so forth as its objects.
For it cannot be maintained that something is produced there by cognition, because [the object] is non-existent.
Nor is it logical to maintain that something is produced which serves as a substratum for the universal of those properties.
Because by that [means], that very [object] would attain the status of being the object [of cognition].

If it is argued that because of identity (*tādātmya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*) is also known as that same [cognition], then is the taste also known when a jar is being cognized by the eye, due to identity?
If it is argued that this [taste] is indeed known in the form of a jar, then why is it not known in the form of taste?

If you say it is because it does not serve as the locus for the imposition of "knownness" (*jñātatā*) in that form, then there would likewise be no knowledge of the past, future, and so forth within a present cognition of a universal (*sāmānya*).
"Because it does not possess the quality of manifestness (*prākaṭya*) in that form. [Ku.
4.513] Now, one might argue: "Since there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that 'by means of an action, something must be produced in the object,' let there be an inference.
No; because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*).
Nor is action here a logical mark (*liṅga*), because it is non-conclusive or unestablished;
nor is there a perceptual experience of anything additional, since [the cognition] merely manifests that specific quality (*vaiśiṣṭya*). (3)

If [the word "produced"] were used with the intention of referring merely to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of conjunctions and so forth;
for nothing at all is produced in the sky by the conjunction with an arrow, nor is anything produced in sound by the manifestation of the final sound.
If it is intended in the sense of vibration, it is unestablished;
if it is intended in the sense of activity, there is deviation due to the activities of words, logical marks, and the senses.
For by those [means of knowledge], nothing at all is produced in the object of cognition;
rather, it is produced in the cognizer alone.
This is likewise true even with respect to the intended result.
Ultimately, because of non-exclusivity due to that very [reason], and because of infinite regress;
this is said with the intention of referring to things whose nature is to perish quickly.
Because there is no fixed rule regarding duality and so forth;
[this is said] with the intention that [the action] is performed quickly,
since the object of the action has not yet been established.
Indeed, what is to be established is simply that knowledge is "active" and "quick-acting";
for the quality of being quick-acting in the agent is not pervaded by its being an auxiliary to the object,
since there are counter-examples in the operations of sound and so forth.
[Ku. 4.514] (3) This might be the case: it could be argued that "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*) is indeed established by experience.
For instance, in general one thinks, "This object is known," and in particular, "This object is directly perceived";
thus, some qualifier of the object itself appears clearly. If this is the objection:
That is incorrect.
For as it is said: "Indeed, the distinction among cognitions arises solely through their objects, since they themselves lack form";
so too, "indeed, the distinction among actions in worldly transactions arises solely through their activities. (4)
Do you not see that,
just as one speaks of "the action of a pot" and "the action of a cloth," so too one says "the pot has been made" or "the pot will be made"?
Understand it in exactly this way.
Just as one says "the cognition of a jar" or "the cognition of a cloth," one says "the jar was known," "the jar will be known," or "the jar is being known.

If you ask how there can be a relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between two things that are unconnected, [we reply]: it is just like saying "the jar is destroyed" (*dhvasta*).
If you ask how even this is possible, [we reply]: surely you have resolved to assert that something is produced in the jar by its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) as well!

If it is argued that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)—whose own definition is dependent upon the definition of that [object]—is "belonging to" that object by its very nature, so what need is there for another relation here? [We reply: It is exactly the same in the case at hand as well.
(4) By this, the objection that "an object cannot be an *karman* because it does not serve as a substratum for a result" is refuted;
for that status is established through being the objective domain of the operation of the instrument (*karaṇa*), just like that which is to be destroyed.
And the status of being a determiner of its own natural fruit is equal [in both cases].
(5) Now, one might object: since cognition is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is to be inferred from its specific effect; in the absence of that [effect], how could it be inferred?

And how could that which is unperceived enter the path of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)? It is for this reason—namely, because the linguistic usage of cognition would otherwise be inexplicable—that "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is postulated.
That too is incorrect, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*):

for knowledge would have to be inferred by means of its "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), and once that [object] is known, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for its linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would make that [cognizedness] known.
[ku.4.517] And for what reason is cognition supersensible?
If it is argued that it is because it is not perceived by the sense organs, we say no; for this would apply to the case of inference as well.
Because it would be indistinguishable from the probandum itself.
However, if one were to put forward mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) without qualification, how could that—unqualified by "fitness" (*yogyatā*)—indicate the absence of sensory perception?
But if it is so qualified, how can cognition be said to be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)?
If it is argued that [the object] is not the locus of such a "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), we say no—because the locus is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

If it is argued that the locus is established precisely by the fact that otherwise linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would be inexplicable, we say no—because that usage is explained by the cause of cognition itself.

If it is argued that this is not so because, even when that cause—in the form of the contact between the self and the mind—is present, there is an absence of linguistic usage regarding objects during deep sleep, we say no—because that alone is not the cause of linguistic usage.
Otherwise, this would be equally applicable even if one accepts [the existence of] cognition.
If it is argued that memory is otherwise inexplicable, we say no—because that too is unestablished.
At any rate, there exists a cause for conventional usage.
If you say "something [is known]," what follows from that?
For by this much alone it is not established that cognition is that [object], since that very [cognition] remains unestablished.

Even so, since there is activity on the part of a determinate agent, it must be by some property of the agent that the cause of activity exists—if this is argued, let desire be admitted as established by perception;
however, knowledge is not [so established].
How then could that very [desire] reside in a determinate locus?
If it is argued that "let it arise," we say no; for this would apply equally even if cognition were admitted.
If it is argued that it arises from some specific cause of its own, then let the desire itself arise from that very cause—what is the use of postulating a cognition?

It might be argued as follows: indeed, the desire to acquire an object arises only when that object is manifest, and not when it is unmanifest during the state of deep sleep—this is established by experience.
Therefore, one must postulate some distinct cause for desire [other than mere manifestation].

If you argue that when [ignorance] exists, the indifference toward objects characterized by deep sleep ceases for the self— alas, by thus asserting that the cessation of deep sleep is established through experience, you must admit that knowledge itself constitutes immediacy (*aparokṣya*);
for one who is not conscious is called "asleep," and the cessation of non-consciousness is precisely consciousness, which is knowledge.
And thus, the reason is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). By this, the argument "because of momentariness" is refuted.
Furthermore, what indeed is this so-called "momentariness"?
If it means perishing very quickly, then it is inconclusive;
if it means persisting for only a single moment, [then...]
That is unestablished, because there is a lack of valid proof.
Now, one might ask: does consciousness, which arises grasping a certain momentary object as stable, grasp that very same [object] in the second moment as well?
Or whether it be otherwise, or not anything at all—
[in any case], the first [alternative] is not tenable.
Because that moment has already passed,
and because perceptual cognition pertains only to the present;
nor does it represent the past as being present.
Because it would follow that [the cognition] is erroneous;
nor is the second [alternative] possible, because it is impossible for there to be an operation after having ceased.

The followers of the Mahāvrata argue that even if one were to accept it as such from the very beginning, it would entail the consequence of looking toward the future; nor is the third [alternative] possible, because it would result in the loss of its status as knowledge.
That is incorrect.
For it is not accepted that cognition grasps an object;

rather, the accepted view is that the cognition itself is the grasping. And thus, whatever object a cognition has taken as its focal point when it first arose, [it is that very object which is subsequently grasped].
The meaning of the question is whether, in the second moment as well, that [cognition] has precisely that [object] as its objective support.
In this regard, the ultimate truth is that it indeed has that as its objective support;
and thus, there is no error.
Because of the failure to penetrate [the truth] due to perversion.

Even so, one might ask: "If the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) has ceased, how can cognition (*jñāna*) continue? Or, if cognition continues, how can the object of knowledge have ceased?"—what is impossible in this case?
For knowledge and the object are neither a single reality nor a single life-span.
Or, even if momentariness were granted, how could [the object] be imperceptible? It is as follows: it is said that [knowledge] is not self-luminous.
Because it is a real entity, like any other real entity;
nor is it graspable by another cognition,
because that [other cognition] does not exist at the same time, given the refutation of the simultaneity of cognitions.
If it is argued that at the time of the apprehender (*grāhaka*), the apprehended (*grāhya*) is past and thus cannot appear as present,
and at the time of the apprehended, the apprehender is future— then indeed, even "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) would not be perceptible,
because of its momentariness.
How so? It is thus: [the future object] is not self-luminous because it is a real entity, nor is it graspable by its producer because it is yet to come.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for [the object] to have ceased its activity,
it cannot be grasped by a cognition that arises at the same time [as the object], since there is no experience of a connection with the sense faculty that produces that cognition. (221)
Nor is it graspable by a subsequent cognition,
because at that time it has already passed away.
If it is asked, "From what [source] does its momentariness itself derive?"— it is from the very reasoning you yourself have stated.
For instance: depending upon which moment they have arisen, do they thereafter depend upon that very same [moment], or another, or none at all?
In this regard, it is not the first case.
Because that [object] does not exist at that time;
nor is it the second [alternative], because there is no transition [of the consciousness].

Furthermore, since knowledge that apprehends a single moment would have as its result a "knownness" (*jñātatā*) residing in other moments, it would follow that such knowledge is erroneous, just like the knowledge of a shell-silver (*rajata*) which has as its result a "knownness" residing in the object present before one.
Nor does cognition penetrate even another moment, because at that time [the first moment] no longer exists.
Nor is it the third [alternative], for that would entail the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
For at that time, it cannot be said whether it belongs to that [object] or to something else.
If you argue that it persists as characterized by that very same past moment—then, in that case, the manifestation would not have a present object.
Otherwise, what fault would there be in cognition also persisting in such a manner?

For there is no such thing as a cognition’s manifestation of the present other than its connection with the illumination of a present object. If that were the case merely by the persistence of an illumination independent of the object, then it would follow that even a cognition whose objects are past or future would likewise manifest the present. [Kārikā 4.522] Now, if one should accept the position that this fault must not arise, and thus that only a grossly present object is apprehended by the illumination—
In that case, since that very same object would be the object of that cognition as well, it too would not be momentary.
Now, if cognition were produced by the sense organs,
there would be no shifting of the object.
Because a relationship has already been established;
nor can there be a restriction based on a restriction of inquiry,
since that inquiry is preceded by doubt.

And because that [cognition] must be preceded by a cognition of the subject (*dharmin*), and because there would be an infinite regress whether the subject is known merely through its presence or through a desire to know it— that is not so, for the same difficulty applies even to the theory of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*). For if that too were an object of knowledge, it would lead to an infinite series of cognitions.
Furthermore, a rule of inquiry (*jijñāsā-niyama*) is likewise untenable in that case;

nor is it reasonable to claim that the cessation [of cognition] results from the severance of the connection with the sense organs, because this would fail to account for the manifestation of the self.
By its very nature, some [object], even if not intended to be inquired about, is known.
If it is argued that this does not apply to all cases—that is, if one says: "It is the same [for us];

one who has a desire to know generated by the recollection of a previously arisen 'knownness' (jñātatā), and who has opened his eyes, perceives only after desiring to know the manifestation (prākaṭya) produced by the arising of knowledge; therefore, there is no infinite regress"—then this is equally [applicable] to our position.
[Ku. 4.524] Now, it may be objected: knowledge is not graspable by conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), because that is preceded by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*);
for what has been grasped by non-conceptual cognition does not persist for even that long [a duration sufficient for conceptualization].
Because it perishes by that very [process],

nor is it cognizable by pure non-conceptual cognition alone, since the latter is inferred by the former and there would be no means of valid cognition for its existence in the absence of that [conceptual cognition].

Nor is it tenable that cognition, like inherence or non-existence, can be the object of a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) independent of an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). For in those cases, such a relationship is possible because the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) is apprehended prior [to the qualified], as is the case with inference and so forth.

In the present instance, however, since properties such as "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) are not perceived, and since a cognition whose qualifier has not been apprehended cannot transition to the qualified (*viśeṣya*), how could this be the case?
No; because as soon as it has arisen, the cognition of an external object performs mere observation (*ālocana*);
then, immediately following that, there occurs at the very first moment the conceptualization (*vikalpana*) of another cognition of the same class.
At that same time, the contact with the sense faculty achieves the perfection of its auxiliary cause, which consists in the grasping of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
For even though a universal is inherent in another individual, it is that very same [universal] which, having been apprehended, is useful [for cognition].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that conceptual cognitions such as inference could not arise;

for since the qualifier residing in that [other individual] has not been apprehended, and that which resides in another [individual] is useless, what could serve as an auxiliary to the apprehension of the logical mark (*liṅga*)?
By this, the perception of sound and so forth is explained.
It might be argued:
(6) for cognition is held to be defined by its object.

Furthermore, there is no perception by the mind of supersensible entities such as atoms; nor can that which is not apprehended function as a qualifier; nor can that which is eternally beyond the senses be the object of a non-sensuous qualified cognition.
Regarding the objection "because of contradiction":
no, for the mind perceives only that which has been presented by a prior cognition, whether it be graspable by an external sense organ or ungraspable;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the recollection of supersensible objects could not arise.

However, this is the distinction: when that [object] exists, [the cognition arises] by its power alone; but when it does not exist, it arises by the power of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by it.
And this being the case, it is not a memory.
Because it is not the object of a cognition that has already been grasped,
and it is not tenable to claim that it is so in respect to its objective aspect— since it appears as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) just like its prior state—
and furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) does not have the dual form of perception and memory, because that would be contradictory.
Now, what is the causal apparatus for perception and recollection?
For perception, it is the additional sensory contact with the object; for recollection, the causal contact consists of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone.
Now, even though it is a form of apprehension, why does it have this direct (aparokṣa) aspect?
Because it is produced by a sense faculty that possesses a contact superior to [ordinary] mental impressions (saṃskāra), without depending on any other cause.
Now, what is proximity (saṃnikarṣa)?
It is inherence in that which is conjoined with cognition (jñāna),
and it is the state of being a qualifier inherent in that which is conjoined with its object.

If it is argued that if the mind were independent [of the senses] in its external operation, it would follow that there would be no such things as the blind or the deaf— this objection does not apply with respect to that which delimits cognition.
For "externally" is not defined in relation to cognition,
nor is independence defined in relation to the object of that cognition.
Because it depends upon that very cognition.
Furthermore, what is the proof for the statement that "cognition is perception"?
Perception itself.
As he formulated: "Because of the internal awareness of the existence or non-existence of conceptual cognitions" (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.31).
Now, one might object: "The cognition of God is not valid knowledge (*pramā*), because, being eternal, it lacks the nature of a result."
Nor is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is not an agent of action;

for this very reason, it is not the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who has that [cognition] as its locus. It is said: "Cognition (*miti*) is correct determination, and the state of being a cognizer is the possession of that [cognition]."
Therefore, in the system of Gautama, validity consists in the exclusion of non-connection [with the object]. (5)
For it is established that valid cognition (*pramā*) is indeed correct experience (*samīcīna-anubhava*).
And thus, the qualification "by way of impermanence" (*anityatvena*) is purposeless; because once the existence of eternal experience is established, there is no desire to exclude it.
And because there is no object to be excluded if [the reason] is unestablished;
nor is this an inference,
since it is subject to either the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) or contradiction (*bādha*).
It is indeed accepted that this [mind] is not the instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks a connection with the valid cognition itself;
rather, the status of being a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) for its substratum consists precisely in its inherence (*samavāya*) therein.
However, the qualification "provided that it is a causal factor" (kārakatve sati) should be understood as being purposeless, just as before.
If this is so, there would be a contradiction with the sūtra: "On account of the authority of the trustworthy person" (Nyāya-sūtra 2.1.68).

If it is argued that, for this reason, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of God is established, but not His status as a knower (*pramātṛtva*), we say no; for there is no contradiction in the application of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) through the presence of its cause.
Indeed, the inherence of valid cognition (*pramā-samavāya*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "knower."
The relationship [of God] with valid cognition, through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), is the cause for the conventional usage of "valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*).
And both of these [valid cognition and its usage] exist in God.
Here too, the qualification "as an effect" should be understood as being useless, just as in the previous case.

[Ku. 4.528] It might be argued as follows: "That by which something is measured is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); that which measures is a cognizer (*pramātṛ*). Thus, since these two are words denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*), how can the object (*artha*) be a non-factor? To this we say: No; for these [derivations] are merely based on the occasion of their etymological formation.
The ground for the application [of the term], however, is exactly as previously shown, because it is established in that way;
otherwise, there would be no conventional usage of the term "cognizer" (pramātṛ) with respect to people such as ourselves.
Because there is a lack of independence in all cases;
although the conventional usage of the term "instrument" (karaṇa) elsewhere may have other causes, here it is intended solely with reference to the cause already mentioned.
In that case, if a fifth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted, it would constitute a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

For it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*), because it does not have the senses, a logical mark (*liṅga*), or words as its instruments. [Response: No, for it is included within perception because it possesses the nature of a direct (*sākṣātkārin*) valid cognition.
Furthermore, because the property of "being produced from the contact of a sense faculty with its object" has as its scope only worldly (empirical) cognition.
It might be argued: even so, the knowledge of Īśvara is not valid cognition (*pramā*), because it is an error (*viparyaya*).

Indeed, when this [cognition] takes the errors of ourselves and others as its object, it is impossible for it to penetrate into knowledge without touching upon its own object; therefore, even that [error] must be admitted as an object.
And thus, that too is a misconception (*viparyaya*).
Because it has a distorted object as its basis,

or because, if that [distortion] were not apprehended, the teachings intended to pacify the delusions of people like us— who are ignorant— would not be preceded by an omniscient being; this is not so, because even though the delusion itself lacks authority, it is non-erroneous insofar as it delineates the reality of its own object.
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total eradication of error, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition [to establish it].

If it is asked: "Even so, since [the object] is the objective support of a cognition delimited by a superimposed object, how is it not erroneous?"—we say: no, because the meaning of "error" is the apprehension of something in a place where it does not exist.
And this [cognition] has that very thing as its object, because it is thus characterized by being in accordance with reality in every respect;
for it is not the case that it is not silver,
nor is it non-existent there.
Nor is it the case that this is not understood:

"In the direct perception (*sākṣātkārin*), which is eternally present, established without dependence on another means, and fixed upon the experience of the real object, all [conceptual elaborations] have ceased. (4.530)
The sequence of the topics.
For me, whose husks of doubt have fallen away through the departure of malice, what need is there for others who are stained by the emergence of suspicion? Śiva alone is my authority. //6//
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Nyāyakusumāñjali. //4//
